forces: Tenor soloist, mixed chorus and orchestra
performers: Michel Sénéchal, tenor; Chorale Élisabeth Brasseur; Orchestre des Concerts Lamoureux; Igor Markevitch, conductor
intro: Low voices begin Boulanger’s prayer for the happiness of every living being; a solo flute and Michel Sénéchal’s tenor take it up in turn. The quiet chant eventually fills the whole choir and orchestra.

sections.label: A · Altos and basses chant
sections.mNote: Repeated Gs in the voices over a C-centred accompaniment

sections.label: B · The flute sings freely
sections.mNote: Solo flute above harps and divided strings

sections.label: C · One tenor carries the prayer
sections.mNote: Bowed and plucked strings alternate beneath the solo voice

sections.label: D · Choir and strings in octaves
sections.mNote: The full choir takes the chant after a long pause

sections.label: Coda · Wordless voices, accelerating orchestra
sections.mNote: Repeated notes accelerate towards the final chord

cues.title: A chant on G
cues.text: Altos and basses begin together, returning insistently to G. The accompaniment rests around C, with the lowered second, D♭, giving the chant its Phrygian sound. Boulanger asks the singers for grave, simple — solemn and simple.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, plate D. & F. 10090, p. 1; Konstantin Galluhn’s preface (2010) identifies the opening Phrygian mode on C and repeated G. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/44/IMSLP21037-PMLP48704-Boulanger_Vielle_Pri%C3%A8re_Bouddhique.pdf https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/987.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A prayer for everyone
cues.text: Suzanne Karpelès supplies Boulanger with the French text in 1914. Its prayer embraces every breathing creature, women and men, gods and humans, east and west, north and south. Each is to overcome suffering and move freely along its own path.
cues.evidence: Translator’s credit on the Durand score, p. 1; French text and the date it reached Boulanger in Konstantin Galluhn’s preface (2010). https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/987.html

cues.title: The flute takes the chant
cues.text: The choir’s last notes linger while a solo flute picks up its phrases. Boulanger asks for the flute to sing freely. Grace notes and quick runs open out the chant above harps, plucked violas and trembling divided violins.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 8–10, flute interlude from bar 36: laisser la Flûte chanter librement, grace notes, harps, divided violin tremolo and pizzicato violas.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A tenor, calm and clear
cues.text: Michel Sénéchal takes the third stanza, marked calme et clair. The divided strings alternate bowed and plucked notes beneath his line. The prayer reaches women, men and fallen beings; its most troubled chords surround the words about those who have fallen.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 11–14, tenor solo from bar 48. Konstantin Galluhn’s preface singles out the dissonant setting of ceux qui sont déchus in bars 57–59.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Rome to Arcachon
cues.text: Boulanger begins the score in Rome in 1914 and finishes it at Arcachon, on the Atlantic coast, in 1917. Both places appear on the last page. She never hears the finished work in concert; Henri Büsser conducts its première on 9 June 1921.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, p. 24, dated Rome 1914 / Arcachon 1917; composition and première history in Konstantin Galluhn’s preface (2010). https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/987.html

cues.title: From humming to full choir
cues.text: Closed-mouth humming leads into a long held pause. Then the full choir and strings proclaim the chant in octaves. The strings remove their mutes; the voices are marked clamant, crying out, as the prayer turns to east, west, north and south.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 17–18: bouches fermées, long fermata, unmuted strings and full choir marked ff clamant.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One last wordless cry
cues.text: The words end, and the choir continues on open vowels. Repeated notes accelerate through the orchestra; harps sweep down with the winds. At Large the rush broadens into a held chord, which swells to fortississimo.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 23–24, coda from bar 98: Accel., wordless Ah, descending harp and wind figures, Large and final crescendo.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The flute continues the last syllable
transitions.how: The choir holds its last syllable while the bass moves into a new chord. At a Tempo the solo flute begins above repeated harp notes, plucked violas and divided violins trembling over the fingerboard. The chant’s short phrases acquire grace notes and runs as the harmony moves away from its opening C.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 8–10, bar 36 onwards: a Tempo, sustained choral syllable, solo flute, harp figures, pizzicato violas and violin tremolo marked sur la touche.

transitions.title: A voice after the flute
transitions.to: C · One tenor carries the prayer
transitions.how: A Cédez slows the flute’s run before figure 4. At a Tempo the tenor enters, calme et clair. The violins and violas divide between bowed and plucked notes; cellos and basses sustain the slower-moving foundation while bass clarinet and bassoons hold their chords.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 10–12, figure 4: Cédez, a Tempo, tenor entry and divided arco/pizzicato strings.

transitions.title: A pause before the cry
transitions.from: C · One tenor carries the prayer
transitions.to: D · Choir and strings in octaves
transitions.how: The voices hum over held wind chords and a descending harp run. A fermata marked long suspends them. The choir then begins in octaves, ff clamant, with the unmuted strings; low winds, trombones and basses reinforce the next sustained chord.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 17–18: humming, long fermata, ff clamant entry and strings instructed to remove mutes.

transitions.title: The vowels carry on
transitions.from: D · Choir and strings in octaves
transitions.how: The choir leaves its final syllable for an open Ah. Winds repeat accented notes above a descending bass, and Accel. drives the orchestra onwards. A downward sweep in harps and winds reaches Large; the choir holds its chord while brass, strings and percussion swell around it.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 23–24: wordless coda, accelerating repeated notes, descending bass and harp figures, then Large and crescendo.

source.title: Lili Boulanger, Vieille prière bouddhique, Durand full score, plate D. & F. 10090
source.locator: Printed pp. 1, 8–12, 17–18, 23–24. The full score includes trumpets, sarrusophone and two harps. A footnote permits six tenors to sing the tenor solo.

timeline.note: Altos and basses begin together over held harp and string chords, with clarinets and horns taking up their phrase.
Sopranos and tenors hum above the words sung by altos and basses.
A solo flute continues the chant above two harps and divided strings.
The tenor enters, calm and clear, above strings divided between bowed and plucked notes.
The choir takes up the tenor’s phrases in imitation, then hums over the strings.
After a long pause, choir and unmuted strings proclaim the chant in octaves, with low brass and percussion.
Wordless voices rise above accelerating wind and string figures. The final chord broadens and swells.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying work clearance is not established: Boulanger died in 1918, but the French translator Suzanne Karpelès died in 1968.
fields.note: A separate ordinary life-plus-70 calculation would put Boulanger’s music out of term, but Karpelès’s translation term would run through 2038. Directive 2011/77/EU also provides a last-survivor term when words and music were specifically created for the same composition; whether that condition applies here has not been established. No permission or applicable text exception is established. The programme’s sound-recording rule 3 is satisfied separately; phonogram expiry is not underlying-work clearance. No lyrics or their translation are reproduced in the guide.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU sound-recording public domain: lawful publication documented by 1960, before 1963.
fields.note: The original commercial mono release LPBR 6059 is dated 1960; the sleeve carries ©1960 Belock, corroborated by the label discography. The rule concerns first lawful publication anywhere, not first EU publication. On the former fifty-year term this phonogram was no longer protected before the 2013 extension. US recording status is not established. No worldwide public-domain claim, Creative Commons licence or modern-remaster release is inferred.

composer.epithet: At nineteen she won the Prix de Rome; before her death at twenty-four she had written songs of lost love and psalms that shake the room.
facts: Ernest and Raïssa Boulanger’s younger daughter; Nadia’s sister
Paul Vidal for composition; Georges Caussade for counterpoint; Nadia at home
First woman to win the Premier Grand Prix de Rome in composition, 1913
Songs, psalms, chamber and orchestral music; unfinished opera La Princesse Maleine
composer.background:
At the Château de Compiègne in May 1913, five young composers were shut away writing a cantata about Faust and Helen of Troy. Someone had sent champagne. Their joint letter of thanks to the composer Fernand Halphen, dated 31 May and written out by Claude Delvincourt, called them “your young colleagues imprisoned in the château to sing the loves of Faust and Helen”. Among the signatures was Lili Boulanger’s. She was nineteen, and this was her second attempt at the Prix de Rome. Illness had forced her to withdraw the previous year.

In July she became the first woman to win the Premier Grand Prix for musical composition. Thirty-one of the Académie des Beaux-Arts’ thirty-six voters supported her. Faust et Hélène gave them a tenor in love with a woman summoned from antiquity, a mezzo-soprano Helen and a baritone devil, all carried by a substantial orchestra. The compulsory text was Eugène Adenis’s adaptation of Goethe. Lili dedicated the score to Nadia, who had won a second prize in 1908.
